source_refs.note: Topic 7.2, printed pages 169-170: the principle and the four steps of X-ray crystallography.

blocks.text: X-ray crystallography was developed in 1912 by William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg, who were awarded the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work. Since then it has been used to analyse diverse substances including minerals, salts, metals, proteins, carbohydrates, nucleic acids and vitamins. In this technique an X-ray beam strikes a crystal, and the atoms and molecules in the crystal diffract the beam in specific directions. From the angles and intensities of the diffracted beams a 3D picture of the electron density within the crystal is produced, and the electron density is used to create the 3D structure of the molecule.
How a protein structure is determined

items: Protein crystallisation: a purified protein is turned into a solid crystal. Crystals are needed because they arrange the protein molecules in a regular, repeating pattern, which is important for getting a clear image in the X-ray process. Scientists slowly mix the protein with special solutions that make the molecules stick together in an orderly way; this can take hours, days or weeks and often needs careful control of temperature, pH and salt concentration. Once a clear, stable crystal has formed it can be used in the next steps.

Production of a diffraction pattern: the good-quality crystal is mounted in the X-ray machine and the X-ray beam is bombarded at it at various angles. The atoms in the crystal diffract the beam and a diffraction pattern, a series of spots, is created on the detectors.
Creating the density map: the angles and intensities of the spots contain information about the arrangement of atoms in the crystal, and the diffraction pattern is used to make a density map.
Determination of the protein structure: the data are analysed mathematically with computational programs, whose calculations transform the data into the 3D structure of the protein.

blocks.alt: Four steps left to right: a purple grid representing a protein crystal; an X-ray source firing a beam at it; a black detector plate with a pattern of white spots; green contour lines of an electron density map; and a green blob with a ribbon inside for the final 3D structure.
blocks.caption: The steps of X-ray crystallography (original diagram after Figure 7.3).
blocks.long_description: A purified protein is first crystallised so that its molecules sit in a regular repeating pattern. X-rays fired at the crystal are diffracted by its atoms into a pattern of spots on a detector, recorded at many angles. The angles and intensities of the spots give a map of the electron density in the crystal, and computer programs turn that density into the three-dimensional structure of the protein.

X-ray beam fired at the crystal at many angles
A pattern of spots on the detectors
Angles and intensities of the spots analysed
The 3D atomic structure of the protein

blocks.prompt: Why cannot a protein in solution simply be placed in the X-ray beam, and what is the first thing a crystallographer must do?
blocks.explanation: Molecules in solution are randomly arranged and scatter X-rays into a blur; only a crystal, where the molecules repeat in a regular pattern, gives sharp diffraction spots. So the first step is to grow a crystal of the purified protein, which may take hours to weeks under controlled temperature, pH and salt concentration.

items: X-ray crystallography (the Braggs, 1912; Nobel Prize 1915) finds 3D structures of minerals, salts, metals, proteins, carbohydrates, nucleic acids and vitamins.
Steps: crystallise the protein; collect the diffraction pattern of spots at many angles; build the electron density map from the angles and intensities; compute the 3D structure.
